articles.title: Slow-Motion Atomic Bomb
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In some sense, all of us on this planet of... well, I was going to say ours, but I’m not so sure anymore... are living through a slow-motion cataclysm, a first-class global apocalypse in the making. As a headline on the World Meteorological Organization’s website put it recently , “State of the climate in 2026 gives new meaning to phrase ‘off the charts.’” Here in the United States in the age of Donald Trump, though, you’d hardly know it. You might even say that, in some sense, the subject is MIA or missing in action. Count on this: If even one atomic bomb were ever to be used in a war in this world of ours, it would be the headline story across this country and planet. And yet, though seldom thought of that way, climate change is essentially the equivalent of a slow-motion atomic attack on this very planet of ours. However, in the age of Donald Trump, who grabs the headlines day after endless day, it goes remarkably unnoticed. Related: Trump, Climate Change, and the Decline of the American Empire It seems to matter little that the weather is already setting new heat records regularly or, as U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said all too vividly recently: “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.” Whether you think about it or not, believe me, it’s happening and, barring surprising action, it’s going to be a first-class nightmare for our children and grandchildren. Imagine this: the other day, November 7th to be exact, for the first time this fall I added a sweater to my very light jacket and shirt on my morning walk here in New York City and also switched from khakis to blue jeans. (The very next day, however, that sweater was gone and I was back in those khakis.) As it happens, I have yet to put on my fall leather jacket, which, once upon a time, I would normally have started wearing daily by at least mid-October (if not before). Buy the Book Not in 2026, though, not on this already distinctly overheating planet of ours. Or as the World Meteorological Society reminds us , “The past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. The global average surface temperature for January–September 2026 was about 1.47 °Celsius above the pre-industrial average. This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December.” Whew! I’m already sweating! In fact, while I was writing this piece, the United Nations Climate Change Conference’s annual summit, known as COP31, was underway in Turkey with 197 countries attending. However, my country and “my” president—shock! shock!—didn’t send a delegation. (Some congressional Democrats did attend , but without the usual State Department assistance!). And if you didn’t even notice, I’m not faintly surprised. After all, it was covered in the media here in an exceedingly modest fashion. This old guy, for instance, still subscribes to and reads (on paper, believe it or not!) the New York Times and it did cover the start of that conference. Its article on the subject , however, was relegated to page 10 of the paper on a day when (of course!) the major front-page headline article was about YKEW (You Know Exactly Whom): “Clear Message to Trump, But Hazy Future for U.S., Parties Face a Gap Until His Term Ends.” And the theme of that article was all too apt after the Republican midterm election losses: “Mr. Trump may be wounded, but a wounded animal can thrash around powerfully.” After a fashion, the climate did manage to sneak onto that paper’s front page in an area at the bottom right headlined , “War Both Slows and Advances Quest for an Energy Transition.” (Note, by the way, that both headlines were different in the online version of the paper.) Related: Welcome to Trumpworld, Where Political Reality Defies Belief Unfortunately, one way “our” president does indeed continue to thrash around is exactly in terms of the climate, and that story, as I mentioned, was relegated to page 10. Think, in fact, of climate change as essentially missing in action in our all-American news world. And yet, although seldom thought of that way, it should essentially be considered the slow-motion equivalent of an atomic attack on this planet. Unfortunately, in the age of Donald Trump, who all too literally grabs the headlines, day after endless day, who among us would be interested in anything happening in such relatively slow motion? Certainly not our president who, only recently in a typical ramble , began on the subject of transgender athletes, then wandered to George Washington’s possible thoughts on the subject. (”George Washington lived in sanity. He didn’t have men playing in women’s sports. I promise you this. I didn’t know George Washington personally, but they did not have the mutilization of your children for transgender purposes.”) Next, he moved on to how a young man from Israel had asked him who his favorite president was, leading him to Abraham Lincoln and only then concluding—if that’s faintly the word for it with him!—this way: “‘Oh.’ I said, ‘That’s nice.’ We love Abraham Lincoln. But you’re going to see something later, because they have a poll—they took a poll recently. You’re going to see it. But I also declared a national emergency on energy and terminated the Green New Scam, one of the greatest hoaxes in the history of our country.” Ah, it’s all clear now, right? Our Scamster-in-Chief, a modern Abraham Lincoln, is intent on wiping the Green New Scam from our very attention span. And why not when, having just gotten clobbered in the midterm elections, he promptly appointed Stephen Miller to be his new White House chief of staff? We’re talking, of course, about the major architect of the president’s mass deportation policy, not to speak of his “hardline crackdown on immigration”—you know, the very policy that Trump himself recently admitted “might have been too tough” in election season. A Hell on Earth? And as passingly strange as all of that might be, it’s my personal reminder that this 82-year-old is, day by day, on a distinctly different planet from anything he once knew or imagined. Generally, if you were paying attention to the mainstream news, though, you would hardly know it. For instance, every night I watch the NBC evening news and then the PBS News, and NBC absolutely loves reporting on climate disasters—floods, tornadoes, raging wildfires, you name it, almost any night of the week. But when it comes to truly naming things, endless weeks can pass without anyone on that news crew even mentioning climate change in passing. Now, as I said, I also watch the PBS evening news and when they report on the growing climate disasters in this country and world of ours, they do tend to mention climate change. But it’s seldom the equivalent of headline material. Nor is it, of course, in the paper New York Times , which I still read daily, and which certainly repor ts on the subject, but not faintly the way it reports, of course(!), on that Washington climate disaster, Donald J. Trump. The one mainstream publication I read that, on a daily basis, deals with climate change in a fashion that seems genuinely appropriate is the British paper, the Guardian , which, believe it or not, actually has an online “climate crisis” section featuring new articles just about every day on the subject. As I was writing this very paragraph, in fact, it typically had these three headlines: “ Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push “; “ Tuesday briefing: The world is falling short on climate action. Can Cop31 change that? “; “ High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer,’ UN climate chief tells Cop31 .” Related: Climate Change Is a Slow-Motion Nuclear War—and We're Already Counting the Dead And it even writes up its reports on the climate in a striking fashion. Here’s just a typical sentence from a piece I also read as I was writing this: “The world is heading for an ‘irrecoverable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions, analysis has found.” And yes, we’re in a world where such coverage should make all too much sense to all of us. But normally, when you’re not being hit by the latest heat wave, tornado, or weather disaster of whatever sort, you simply wouldn’t know from most of the media that we’re in a potentially world-destroying situation (at least as we’ve known it all these centuries), just in (relatively) slow motion. Nor, if you live in the United States, would you normally have the faintest idea that, as the Guardian reported recently , “while all the other 20 major economies reduced or slowed their carbon pollution last year, the U.S. was a ‘major exception’ by emitting an extra 133m tons of planet-heating gases from the burning of coal, oil and gas.” Nor, for that matter, would you be likely to know that “heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported as the Cop31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.” Phew! I’m already sweating! So here we are, distinctly in a new age of ever-increasing climate extremes, with a climate-crazed president in the White House and other climate ignorers like Russia’s Vladimir Putin right before our global eyes. Yet, if you’re not listening to someone like U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, you essentially might never truly know it (or at least take it in). And the more we wait to face our present reality, while allowing figures like Trump and Putin to control major countries on this planet, the less likely it is that we’ll be able to deal with that onrushing global future and save ourselves from—all too literally—a hell on Earth.

articles.title: Democracy Strikes Back
articles.author: John Peeler
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I owe Judy Peeler thanks for inspiring this comparison. October 5, 1988: Dictator General Augusto Pinochet is unexpectedly and overwhelmingly defeated in a referendum intended to authorize a second eight-year term as President. After his efforts to hold on to power are blocked by other members of the military junta, Pinochet follows his own rules and stages a general election in 1989 that ends his 16 year dictatorship and restores democracy in Chile after the violent coup that overthrew the last elected president, Salvador Allende, in 1973. April 12, 2026: After a decade in power, Prime Minister Victor Orbán is unexpectedly defeated in a parliamentary election. His previously dominant party is almost wiped out as a parliamentary presence. Peter Magyar, the new prime minister, swiftly erases the authoritarian measures designed to keep Orbán in power, and restores Hungarian democracy. Orbán pioneered techniques of “electoral authoritarianism” designed to retain the trappings of electoral democracy while making opposition victory all but impossible. November 3, 2026: Just two years after the election that returned him to office, President Donald Trump is overwhelmingly rejected in the midterm elections for Congress, state legislatures and governors. In his final two years as President, Trump will face a strongly Democratic House and Senate that will investigate the misdeeds of his regime, check his misuse of funds, and lay the groundwork for a probable Democratic President in 2028. Trump had patterned his electoral authoritarianism on that of Orban. Related: Trump's Political Collapse Was Entirely His Own Making After a generation of democracy in retreat around the world, and ten years when Trump’s right-wing authoritarianism has dominated politics in the United States, we are seeing a resurgence of democracy as evidenced in the defeats this year of Orbán and Trump. The defeat of Pinochet 38 years ago prefigured this resurgence. Indeed, it was in its time a key part of the resurgence of democracy all over Latin America after of decade of brutal right-wing dictatorships that were promoted and protected by the United States. In all three cases the regime was defeated, not by violent uprisings, but by the people’s vote. This was not entirely surprising in the US and Hungarian cases, since both regimes retained the trappings of electoral democracy. But Pinochet was a straight-up military dictator who had ordered the executions and disappearances of thousands of people. Yet even he felt, eventually, constrained to clothe his regime in the legitimacy of the popular vote. He did this by getting popular endorsement of a constitution that would let him rule for eight years, then have a referendum to confirm him in a second eight year term. He obviously assumed that he would prevail in that referendum, hence failed to fix the election. Big mistake. Related: Receivership: Agenda for a Democratic Congress In the last century, democracy has emerged worldwide as the only widely accepted principle of political legitimacy. There are still regimes that defy that principle, including Saudi Arabia and China, but most dictatorships try to clothe themselves in popular consent, even if that consent is coerced. Russia is a prime example. So is Iran. Other legitimacy principles, such as hereditary or religious authority, are just not believed by many people anymore. Without the trappings of popular consent, Pinochet was an emperor with no clothes. Similarly, Orbán and Trump, for all their authoritarian aspirations, had to keep elections, and couldn’t go too far in fixing the outcomes without undermining their legitimacy. Electoral authoritarianism is the attempt to dictate within democracy. Finally, democracy trumped Trump. The crisis of democracy is by no means over. Electoral authoritarians are still entrenched in Russia, Turkey and India, and far-right parties are surging in France and Germany. And it is deeply problematic when only one party defends democracy, as in Brazil and the United States. In the long term, democracy can only thrive when alternation of parties in power does not threaten democracy itself. Still, we are right to celebrate these victories for democracy against the spirit of darkness and division.

articles.title: Rejecting Equality Is a Long-Standing American Tradition
articles.author: Robbie Nelson
articles.content: Living in a country whose residents include both the world’s first trillionaire and 1.5 million homeless schoolchildren, the fact of American inequality is hard to miss. Such a reality produces countless justifications, explanations, and plans for ameliorating its worst impacts across the political spectrum. But at its sharpest edge, it also produces a coterie of intellectuals, pseudo-intellectuals, tycoons, activists, and posters who don’t merely attempt to explain or excuse inequality but rather celebrate its fruits and try to consolidate its bases. Silicon Valley today plays host to the most prominent nest of techno-fascists, neoreactionaries, transhumanists, and “ effective altruists ” whose obscene wealth allows them to shape political discourse far beyond the strengths of their ideas or their personal charms, such as they are. But as Kim Phillips-Fein demonstrates in her new book Country of Lords , the current version of explicitly anti-egalitarian politics adopted by today’s economic and political elites is merely the latest in a long tradition of American reactionary thought. Aimed squarely against the premise announced in the Declaration of Independence that “all men are created equal,” this intellectual and political lineage has been carried forward by the lawyers, business moguls, charlatans, and academics who form the primary figures of Phillips-Fein’s sweeping tour of American political history. Country of Lords is a highly readable book, filled with a cast of colorful characters both well-known and more obscure. It sets forth a counter-history to the sunny, West Wing –style liberal narrative in which the inevitable march of American progress toward equal inclusion only faces obstacles thrown up by the dead weight of tradition or ignorance. Instead, building upon her previous work about the role of right-wing businessmen in fighting against the New Deal, Phillips-Fein shows the strenuous and continuous efforts of reactionary figures not merely to conserve some traditional order but to transform and reestablish new hierarchies in the face of technological, social, and political change. Action and Reaction The book is organized into six primary chapters, arranged chronologically and each anchored around a few historical figures and their connected sets of ideas. The New England statesman John Adams and the racist pro-slavery theorist George Fitzhugh might seem an odd pairing, but Phillips-Fein links their attempts to define the roles of their respective political and racial “aristocracies” in the early decades of American Republic. Likewise with the Yale professor William Graham Sumner and industrialist Andrew Carnegie enunciating their own versions of “survival of the fittest” in the context of Gilded Age industrial society. Next are the “utilitarian racists,” anchored by Lothrop Stoddard and his infamous 1920 book, The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy , a deeply racist cri de coeur (beloved by The Great Gatsby character Tom Buchanan) that identified World War I and the Bolshevik revolution as the tipping points against European colonial power. The interwar period ushered in the age of Henry Ford and his “Gospel of Production,” a corporatist vision of American society in which the unequal unity of proprietors and their loyal workers could box out both the (Jewish-coded) union Reds and the (Jewish-coded) financiers. The book’s fifth chapter, perhaps its most interesting and certainly its most expansive, takes a broader view of postwar liberalism’s discontents. Particularly potent are the various debates around the rise of intelligence quotient (IQ) tests, standardized college admissions exams like the SAT, and ideas about “equality of opportunity” in the midst of the legal changes called forth by the civil rights movements of the 1950s and ’60s. The author eventually hones in on the scientist-turned-racist-crank William Shockley and the Harvard psychologist Richard Herrnstein, two figures associated with the thesis that IQ is heritable and racially differentiated. Phillips-Fein pairs the race-and-IQ crowd with the libertarians and monetarists represented by the likes of Ayn Rand and Milton Friedman. What united these seemingly disparate figures was their belief that purportedly “neutral” mechanisms (standardized intelligence tests and free-market competition) could separate the “natural elite” from those meant to be ruled. The book ends with an investigation of the antidemocratic strains within Silicon Valley that provide a surprising intellectual continuity between the countercultural 1960s to the corporate consolidation of the 1980s and ’90s to the emergence of hard-right tech anti-humanists that dominate the scene today. Each chapter could stand on its own, a mini-history of a particular moment and the multiple strands of anti-egalitarian politics that attended it. But, taken together, they paint a larger picture. By fleshing out both the continuities and similarities between inegalitarian ideas across time, some crucial patterns emerge. Idiosyncratic though they may be, these anti-egalitarian thinkers did not develop their ideas in a vacuum. Rather, their politics are deeply responsive to the emerging shape of struggle from below. In other words, reactionary thinkers are always reactive to historically particular assertions of political power from the lower orders. Although each chapter focuses primarily on conservative ideologues, their antagonists make consistent appearances. In each successive historical moment, new rounds of egalitarian struggle imperiled the ruling order. In response, new reactionary ideologies emerged that sought to both enshrine and update the ideological map of inequality. The story lurking beneath The Country of Lords is that of an episodic but relatively cohesive American egalitarian tradition. From radical Enlightenment thinkers and indebted Revolutionary War veterans to abolitionists, Knights of Labor to the Socialist Party of Eugene V. Debs, garment workers on the Lower East Side to the NAACP of W. E. B Du Bois, United Auto Workers organizers to civil rights activists and beyond, American history has churned out ceaseless waves of agitators and movements seeking to overturn the social, economic, and political order and establish a more equal future. The task of the modern reactionary, then, has not been to simply assert the God-given superiority of certain aristocratic families, but rather to counter each successive challenge with an updated and reorganized hierarchy that fits the changing social, technological, and economic landscapes that they encounter. Henry Ford’s worldview was not atavistic but distinctly modern and technologically driven, in the spirit of his age. His model of American corporatism incorporated not only the revolutionary technologies of internal combustion and the assembly line, but also cutting-edge social-scientific research into managing his workers’ lives and bodies on and off the factory floor. Richard Herrnstein likewise did not subscribe to George Wallace–style Southern segregationism, but rather employed advanced (though subsequently debunked) statistical methods to make his arguments about race and IQ, being careful not to deny the possibility of individual black success stories. In other words, the realities of social mobility, new institutions, and new social attitudes pressurized the shape of these anti-egalitarian ideas. Almost all of these anti-egalitatarian figures relied heavily on the discursive power of science and technology in both their explanations of inequality and their visions of how that inequality could be leveraged for social good. As the primary modern schema for adjudicating differences between things and producing causal explanations for social phenomena, the natural and social sciences loom large in the reactionary imagination as both threats and resources. It is telling that almost all of this book’s subjects were not, themselves, born into high privilege. They ranged from working-class immigrants who worked their way up through industry or academia (Carnegie, Herrnstein, Friedman) to the children of middling farmers (Ford, Adams, Sumner) to the children of moderately successful provincial professionals (Fitzhugh, Stoddard). Interestingly, two of the techno-racists (Shockley and Peter Thiel) are the children of prosperous but highly peripatetic mining engineers. Having gained a vantage point on American society from both outside and inside the elite, these up-and-comers were often able to craft and mobilize ideological concepts that went beyond mere defense of status quo elite configurations. Because of their personal prominence in the American economic or intellectual scene, these individuals had deep investment in both upholding the legitimacy of the system as well as opening that system up to the fresh perspectives of those coming from outside the blue-blood northeastern elite. Potential for upward social mobility of one kind or another is a load-bearing feature of most modern reactionary ideologies, because it both serves to justify the merited existence of a ruling class while also leaving open the possibility of entry. The replenishment of the upper classes and the defanging of disruptive movements from below are the dual goals of these political movements. Constructing Equality Because of its particular focus on the history of anti-egalitarian ideas in the United States as well as its slim profile, Country of Lords does not spend much time building up a competing, left-wing account of and response to inequality. While the Left’s primary political task is countering actual inequality in the workplace, social relations, and the state, we also have to develop our own story about the nature of inequality in order to counter some of the key arguments of the reactionaries and their liberal fellow travelers. There are both empirical observations and normative claims at the heart of this story. First, human beings are not “equal” or equivalent in terms of our physical capacities, desires, and talents. We inhabit different bodies and life experiences. But we assert that human beings do have equal dignity and worth and thus should be given, to the greatest extent possible, equal power to determine our own lives and to participate in decision-making that shapes our societies. The question at play in modern progressive politics is determining which institutions and historical processes can cultivate flourishing egalitarian societies in the context of human diversity and nonequivalency. Historically speaking, unequal social classes are a pretty recent human social phenomenon, only emerging around twelve thousand years ago during the Neolithic revolution. During this era, the advent of agriculture, livestock domestication, sedentary urbanism, and the complex social division of labor fed into the generation of social surplus. In other words, these societies were able to produce and store more food than was necessary to meet their populations’ immediate needs. New elites emerged and solidified their ability to command others’ labor, coordinate production and exchange, and make decisions about how to mobilize that social surplus. These new practices enabled the development of larger human populations, more advanced technology, and greater complexity in social, cultural, and economic life. This rough historical sketch, viewed in a certain way, lends credence to anti-egalitarian arguments: human societies, since the birth of agriculture, have depended in fundamental ways on social hierarchy. In this telling, hierarchical divisions of labor were necessary to produce the technological advancements that have propelled humanity from living as small bands of hunter-gatherers to becoming geo-engineers and star-travelers. However, the anti-egalitarians err in misidentifying the historically functional inequality of class society as an intrinsic inequality. Unequal power over the social surplus was provisionally necessary for the class system as it has emerged, but, empirically speaking, the actual people in those dominant positions over the course of history have not shared any intrinsic biological, moral, or technical superiority over those they have dominated. The socialist movement has thus set for itself the most ambitious task imaginable: the construction of systems that sustain a complex divisions of labor necessary for a technologically advanced mass society — which is comprised of individuals who each have unique capacities and desires — while maintaining roughly equal access to social income and roughly equal decision-making power about the production and distribution of social surplus. An equal future cannot simply be wished or asserted: it needs to be built. Despite Karl Marx’s famous injunction against “writing recipes for the cookshops of the future,” there has been a rash of recent English-language writing attempting to sketch the contours of a socialist future. While each example deserves its own complex treatment — and there are tensions between different visions — the ideas and institutions of democracy lie at the heart of each one. The particular combination and format of representative and direct democratic decision-making is up for contestation, as is the precise role of markets in economic life. But democratic decision-making is the key mechanism for synthesizing the reality of individual difference with the need for collective deliberation and rough equality of political power. In a socialist future characterized by social complexity, division of labor, technological advancement, civil liberties, rough equality of social income, and rough equality of political capacity, democracy is the indispensable technology. articles.title: The Violent Far-Right Response to France’s Protests
articles.author: Olly Haynes
articles.content: For France’s media-political classes, the recent student movement has prompted a series of searching questions about violence and who has the right to use it. Debates often center on the alleged closeness of protesters to La France Insoumise, implying that Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s left-wing party is somehow responsible for vandalism by protesters and marginal acts of violence by students. Less remarked upon however, is that a wave of violence coming from the far right has also marked the protests and the presidential election campaign. Nor has it been much noted that this violence has killed already, and that Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National (RN) is alarmingly close to the violent groupuscules involved. Already on October 24, far-right militants attacked trade unionists and protesters in Rouen, Nice, and Montpellier. In a video taken by a bystander in Rouen, Normandy, members of local identitarian movement Les Normaux can be seen throwing a man to the pavement before kicking him. None of the men were arrested by the police, although officers were present on the scene. The identitarians attempted to intimidate protesters by yelling far-right slogans such as “Rouen, Rouen is nationalist” and “the street and France belongs to us.” The group had launched similar attacks on protesters the week before, beating two people to the ground and leaving them bloody. In a video taken before the incident, a man can be seen at the head of their march, a leather belt wrapped around his fist, metal buckle in hand like a makeshift knuckle-duster. Street Press, a news website that closely monitors far-right activity, identified the man as Mathieu Balavoine, who runs a production company that was hired by the Rassemblement National in 2024, and that last year earned over €100,000 for a contract making videos for the party’s group in the European Parliament. The far right’s propensity for lethal violence has also been demonstrated elsewhere in recent weeks. On October 23, Kevin Tessier, a coked-up fascist armed with an automatic weapon, fired 128 bullets at black and Arab people in the city of Trappes, killing one person and injuring four. Trappes had repeatedly been the subject of a media moral panic about “territories lost to the Republic” because of their large minority populations. Le Pen contributed to this over the years, tweeting in 2018 following a stabbing in the city, that Trappes is “the symbol of those cities and neighborhoods where the French Republic has retreated, making way for communalism and Islamism.” Tessier’s motives were undeniably racist. Whether he was influenced directly by Le Pen’s words is unknown, but stickers found in his house suggest that he was at least a party sympathizer. Among a copy of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf and other items indicative of his far-right ideology, were thirty stickers bearing the words “Long Live France, the RN, proud to be French.” These were just the most recent instances of a longer story of far-right violence in France. In 2022 Argentine rugby player Federico Martín Aramburú was gunned down in the street by two former members of the Groupe Union Défense (GUD), a fascist youth circle with close ties to the RN. In 2023, a wave of far-right violence was unleashed in reaction to the Nahel Merzouk riots, which followed the police killing of a seventeen-year-old. That year, France became the only European country to see a major increase in the number of violent attacks by far-right groups compared to the 2010–2022 national average, according to a study by the Center for Research on Extremism. Since then, acts of violence by such groups targeting ethnic minorities and political opponents have become increasingly common. According to daily Libération , there was an average of one far-right attack per week in 2025. The groups perpetrating these attacks — the formations that emerged following the self-dissolution of the GUD and the mandatory dissolution of Génération Identitaire — are alarmingly close to the RN. According to Thomas Portes, who is president of the National Observatory of the Far Right, and France Insoumise MP for Saint-Denis, “There has been no break between the parliamentary far right and the groupuscules.” [In France] we have an annual mobilization by the May 9 Committee; it’s a Nazi demonstration in homage to a fascist activist who died. It was banned this year, but two years ago, the paperwork for the demonstration was filed by a parliamentary attaché for the RN, called Maylis de Cibon. There was a parliamentary assistant called Raphaël Ayma, who spoke at a conference of the friends of Léon Degrelle, a Belgian Nazi figure [before Ayma was expelled from the RN]. There is the press secretary of the RN group, Elise Laplace, who has just married a neofascist activist that arranged an attack on a political meeting in Bordeaux that was organized by my fellow [France Insoumise] MPs Louis Boyard and Carlos Martens Bilongo. “It goes beyond the assistants,” Portes tells Jacobin , pointing to the case of Tiffany Joncour, an RN MP whose husband, a hooligan with a background in the identitarian movement, beat up her parliamentary assistant whom he suspected of having an affair with her. Portes’s list continues, telling Jacobin about four further examples. Even this list is not exhaustive. While researching another article, in the Eurocom forum that the group organizes through, I found an account of the Save Europe Act, an organization linking identitarian movements across Europe, which includes several groupuscules accused of violence. The account bore the name and location of Philippe Eymery, an RN regional counselor whose party branch was exposed in 2018 for employing Génération Identitaire activists. Eymery recently appeared on a radio show alongside various extreme-right groups that are members of the Eurocom group, promoting remigration. (He did not respond to my message requests on Twitter attempting to confirm if he was the owner of the account with his name.) At France Insoumise’s own summer university in August, the party’s parliamentary chief Mathilde Panot told journalists that this would be an unusual presidential election campaign because of the level of violence that she and her colleagues expected. Her assessment has already proved prescient, though France Insoumise has in fact long been a target for far-right violence. The Trappes killer had a list suggesting he was intending to target France Insoumise MPs David Guiraud and Aymeric Caron, as well as anti-police-violence campaigner Assa Traoré and Green MP Sandrine Rousseau. France Insoumise canvassers and parliamentary assistants have been beaten up while campaigning for Mélenchon, and even the Quentin Deranque affair, which ended with a neo-Nazi activist dying from injuries sustained in a street fight by antifascist activists, began with fascist activists ambushing the antifascist activists outside a France Insoumise meeting in Lyon. According to Portes, there is an “operation to reverse society’s moral compass based on falsehoods, which is targeted against us. For example, yesterday the minister of education tried to claim that it was France Insoumise, our activists and officials, who brought fireworks to high school students to allow them to fire them at school buildings. The interior minister was forced to deny it today. . . . As for the far right, we represent everything that they hate. That is to say the imaginary of an anti-racist, anti-colonial, antifascist, egalitarian, New France.” Part of Marine Le Pen’s strategy of detoxification has been to expel party members associated with openly extreme or violent groups in French politics. However, they only seem to be expelled when the press gets wind of it, and even then those close to the leader can escape unscathed. The Rassemblement National in parliament with the “shirts and ties” is just “decor” and “window dressing” says Portes. “When you look at the list of people who are elected officials for the RN, or their assistants, it’s a nursery of neo-Nazi, nationalist, royalist, and identitarian activists.” Le Pen may have successfully detoxified the party brand. That doesn’t, however, mean that it has actually changed. articles.title: Why Are Most Union Leaders Silent on Booting Chuck Schumer?
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content: Why have only four national unions publicly backed Chris Van Hollen against Chuck Schumer for Senate leader? The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, the Office and Professional Employees International Union, National Nurses United, and the National Union of Healthcare Workers have taken Van Hollen’s side in this urgent fight. But where is everybody else? It’s hard to overstate the stakes. If Democrats once again squander the opportunity given to them by the American people, the lost chance to improve people’s lives — and the ensuing political backlash — could be even worse than what followed the Clinton, Obama, and Biden administrations. Schumer-style corporate politics might as well have been designed in a lab to ensure that Democrats disappoint voters and quickly hand Republicans back the reins of power, perhaps this time under an even more dangerous and effective incarnation of far-right reaction. Missing the Moment There is exactly zero reason to believe Schumer is the man for this moment. He’s a pro-Israel war hawk who is deeply embedded with the same billionaires that Democrats — including every single victorious 2026 Democratic Senate candidate in a battleground state — ran against in these midterms. Want to see the pro-union Protecting the Right to Organize ( PRO) Act and other urgent reforms passed within the first hundred days of the next Democratic administration? So do I. But even if Democrats win the presidency and retain Congress, getting this crucial labor law reform enacted will almost certainly require abolishing the filibuster. Van Hollen has explicitly endorsed doing so. As he put it last Friday , the Senate needs to let majorities govern with “fifty-one votes,” rather than keeping the “antidemocratic” filibuster. Schumer, by contrast, has refused to say whether he’d support getting rid of it. Asked directly after the midterms whether Democrats should abolish the rule, he dodged the question. There’s also plenty a Senate majority leader can do over the next two years, even with Trump still holding the presidential veto. Democrats should aggressively investigate the administration’s corruption and use their control over spending to immediately challenge its worst policies on Iran, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Israel. Even more important, they’ll need to make crystal clear to Americans the ambitious agenda they’ll enact if they win the White House in 2028. Van Hollen is promising to make the Senate a center of political opposition to billionaire power, putting popular reforms on the table and forcing Republicans to defend their opposition. Schumer is itching to return to the familiar routines of Schumerism: decent policy promises, timid negotiations, and endless excuses for inaction. Plus, he’s insanely unpopular. A November YouGov poll found that just 23 percent of voters viewed Schumer favorably, compared with 39 percent for Trump. That’s right: the Democratic leader most national unions are so far refusing to buck is substantially less popular than Donald Trump. An astonishing 57 percent of voters view Schumer unfavorably. Only 10 percent want him to remain Senate majority leader, compared with 57 percent who want somebody else. Why on earth should the party’s future be placed in the hands of someone so widely disliked? Schumer’s supporters understandably point to the Democratic victories this month. He did help recruit some good candidates, and that deserves some credit. But winning a midterm election amid an unpopular president’s economic and political disasters is a pretty different task from governing successfully afterward. The Case for Van Hollen Like Franklin Delano Roosevelt in the 1930s, Van Hollen comes out of the Democratic establishment but is reading the mood of the public and offering a real alternative to politics as usual. He has called for confronting billionaire power, backed Medicare for All, supported ending the filibuster, and taken a much tougher line on using congressional spending authority to end Trump’s war with Iran. He has also pledged to give the new class of insurgent populist senators a greater role in shaping the party’s direction. Obviously, changing the leader won’t automatically overcome every obstacle to reform. Obviously, switching Senate leaders doesn’t mean the rest of us can sit back and watch the Democrats finally deliver. But there’s a big difference between a leader promising to break with business as usual and one whose career has largely been built around it. Van Hollen has also shown that he’s willing to take political risks for workers. Don’t forget the case of Kilmar Ábrego García, the sheet-metal apprentice and International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART) member who Trump illegally deported to a notorious prison in El Salvador. Van Hollen personally flew there, met with Ábrego García, and helped lead the fight that brought him back to the United States. You would think SMART leadership would back a leader willing to go to such a degree for one of its members. Some national unions have so far made clear that they understand the stakes. The Machinists’ president, Brian Bryant, said Van Hollen understood that the fight was one of “Workers vs. Billionaires.” OPEIU likewise sent Schumer a letter urging him to withdraw and make way for another leader, such as Van Hollen. National Nurses United put the point well in endorsing Van Hollen. Its executive director, Puneet Maharaj, warned that Democrats must not squander the opening voters have given them. Politicking on the K Street Corridor The reason why more national union leaders aren’t yet saying the same isn’t complicated. Many of them feel that a significant part of their job is to build close relationships with congresspeople to deliver for their members and fight for pro-worker legislation. If they back Van Hollen and Schumer wins, there’s a real risk that their union might suddenly find that their calls get returned a little less quickly (or not at all), and that important Democratic leaders might no longer listen to their legislative priorities. That’s a valid concern, especially given how Washington currently works. But it’s also an extraordinarily narrow way to calculate political risk, especially at this moment of crisis. For years now, progressive union leaders have rightly insisted that democracy is on the line, that sky-high economic inequality must be reversed, that the Democrats should stand up for the little guy, and that the labor movement must do everything possible to defeat MAGA and greedy CEOs. Now union leaders and Democrats have a rare opportunity to actually move the needle in that direction. And it wouldn’t even take much effort. This Senate fight is one of those exceedingly rare moments when a union press release could make a historic difference for working people and the country as a whole. There’s no excuse for silence. Schumer is seventy-five and faces reelection in 2028 — if he even chooses to run. He’s hardly a permanent fixture of American politics. And Van Hollen is a respected senator who can work across the party’s ideological divisions. The timidity prevailing on the K Street corridor of downtown DC isn’t an inevitable way of doing politics. Just look at how much bolder unions have been in state-level contests this year. In Michigan, the United Auto Workers (UAW), the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) Michigan, National Nurses United, the Association of Flight Attendants, and United Food and Commercial Workers Local 951 were among the unions that took sides in a fiercely contested Democratic Senate primary, backing Abdul El-Sayed against Schumer’s preferred candidate, Haley Stevens. In Maine, the state AFL-CIO and dozens of local unions went all out for Troy Jackson. And in Minnesota, the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), UNITE HERE Local 17, and others backed Peggy Flanagan against the more establishment-friendly Angie Craig. All three of these Senate winners are now supporting Van Hollen. Moving away from this bold spirit, most national union leaders currently appear to want to stay silent, hoping to square the circle between the evident anger of their base and their desire not to break with Schumer. Some of them have framed the issue to me over the past few days as a matter of fighting for the agenda, not the person. But whether they like it or not, it’s precisely that choice of agenda and strategy that’s now being posed by the Senate leadership fight. Everybody knows that who leads the party has a great deal to do with what the party actually does. It’s a bit disingenuous, too, to suddenly insist that the agenda matters but the leadership doesn’t, given how many national unions came out swinging for Nancy Pelosi when her speakership seemed like it might be challenged in 2018. Back then, the AFL-CIO, AFT, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, SEIU, UAW, the United Steelworkers, and numerous other unions publicly backed Pelosi in her fight to return as House Speaker. Union leaders understand that the choice of congressional leadership matters for the legislative agenda. Not Too Late My suggestion to rank-and-file members and local and state union leaders is to look at this Van Hollen–Schumer fight as a test of whether their national leaders are ready to meet the moment. If they’re not able to take even this relatively mild risk to help save the Democrats from themselves, why should we expect them to take on the much bigger, even more consequential risks, like backing anti-corporate candidates for office in 2028 or massively investing in new organizing to unionize America afterward? National union leaders still sitting this out or leaning toward Schumer should reconsider. In today’s fight for the future of the Democratic Party, national unions have to choose a side. They can stick with the old, corporate-friendly hacks who helped get us into this mess, or stand with those willing to fight against business as usual. There’s no neutral ground here. articles.title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms. More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won. United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.” In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate. “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told Michigan Advance . “Michiganders… are telling these people they’re not for sale.” Logger and union member Troy Jackson won a Senate seat against 30-year incumbent Republican Susan Collins in Maine after the UAW and the Maine AFL-CIO helped defeat the establishment choice in the primary there. In Ohio, labor stalwart Sherrod Brown faced a river of crypto lobby cash but recovered the Senate seat he lost in 2024. In Texas, the Communications Workers (CWA) mobilized for union-member candidates up and down the ticket, asking candidates to commit to a “Contract with Working Texans.” Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa signed on—she’s a labor lawyer, member of Texas State Employees Union/CWA, and the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990. Various union members and leaders are headed for Congress. Ironworker Brian Poindexter won in Ohio. Pennsylvanians elected firefighter and union president Bob Brooks. Forest Service smokejumper and local union vice president Sam Forstag won in Montana. VA nurse and union member Mitchell Berman beat a Republican incumbent in Wisconsin. In New York, UAW members and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated establishment Democrats in the primary, then romped November 3. Richard Ojeda, a champion of the West Virginia teachers’ strike of 2018, won a Congressional seat in North Carolina, beating the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. "We were elected to elevate the lives of working people across this country,” said Ojeda . “We're coming in LASER FOCUSED on the mission. Help people. Hold anyone who has hurt people accountable. Tax the billionaires. The end.” Others lost, but came way closer than expected. In Nebraska, Kellogg’s strike leader and independent Dan Osborn came up short (44-50) for U.S. Senate. He faced ferocious attack ads, with $24 million in ‘independent’ spending. In Florida, former SEIU organizer and DSA member Angie Nixon defeated the establishment Democrat in the primary and almost won (48-50) a Senate race the pundits had written off. She got zero support from the national Democratic Party. CORPORATE DEMS UNDER FIRE Now some unions have come out swinging, demanding more from the party. The Machinists (IAM) sent a letter urging Senator Chuck Schumer to resign as party leader . OPEIU did the same . The IAM “is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people,” said President Brian Bryant. “This means… sweeping economic policy changes that will recalibrate the vast, immoral, economic injustice in this country.” The United Electrical Workers concurred: “The credit for these wins belongs not to the Democratic Party—whose leadership has offered at best tepid resistance to the Republican agenda over the past two years—but to the working people across the country who have spent the last two years organizing and fighting back in their communities and workplaces.” UE set out an ambitious agenda : a $25 minimum wage, Medicare for All, dismantling ICE, taxing the rich, protecting Social Security, and passing labor law reform including the PRO Act and card-check recognition for speedier union recognition. National Nurses United said voters expect a stop to health care cuts, stat. President Trump can veto most bills Congress passes, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders insisted on November 9 that Congress needs to do its job and pass a bold working-class agenda. If Trump vetoes the bills, that’ll raise the stakes in 2028 to elect a president who will sign them. It’ll take a lot of pressure get corporate Democrats to defy their paymasters. So plans are afoot for May Day 2028 , when the Auto Workers and other unions have important contracts expiring. The plan is to keep the focus on working class demands, backed by a season of contract campaigns and strikes.

articles.title: ‘Delay, Deny, Discipline’ Is Amazon’s Real Pregnancy Policy, Workers Say
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat… He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit. But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations—a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting. Amazon—a company known for fast delivery—had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day, but no chair. She was moved to a different position, but still required to lift heavy packages. Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at 80 hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation, but stopped because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says. The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up, Amazon fired her. Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave (see box at end of article) . Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by A Better Balance , a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all U.S. workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon. SYSTEMATIC VIOLATIONS Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that. “Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.” Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.) Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant. PATTERN OF ILLEGALITY Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say “yes,” they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say “no,” Amazon puts them on unpaid leave , which rapidly runs out. Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700… I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat. “Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.” Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance has also sued Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.) TRAGIC RESULTS Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly 10-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it. She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse. Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to speak out . Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child. LAW REDUCES MISCARRIAGES When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, a study found that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law. Pregnant With A Contract Postal workers move packages like Amazon warehouse workers do, but they have a union contract. It makes all the difference when you’re pregnant, said Postal Workers (APWU) national field organizer Lori Cash. She hired into a heavy job at the Postal Service in 1998 while pregnant with her third child. After a couple of months, her doctor told her she needed to stop work, but she had no sick leave or vacation time accrued. “I went to my union steward, and I said, ‘This is what my doctor is telling me, I’m scared.’ I had no idea what my rights were. I’d never been in a union before.” Her steward explained that she could take leave without pay, under the contract, and could not be fired: “We have a just cause process in our contract. They have to prove that they had a just reason to fire you, and just using too much time off without being paid is not justified.” After the birth, Cash came back to work, but it was too hard: “I had two toddlers and a newborn. I was trying to go back to work with all those shenanigans going on at my house with all these babies.” She told her steward she was thinking of quitting. But her steward fought for her to get the option to come back with fewer hours and gradually increase them, which was also guaranteed in their contract. “Pregnancy is stressful,” said Cash. “You have so much to worry about.” But during her next pregnancy, she felt “much more confident that I was going to be able to get the accommodations I needed. I had a whole union behind me, fighting to make sure that those rights were given to me, and to make sure that I had a healthy pregnancy and was able to take the time that I needed for me, and for my baby to be taken care of.” But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around 50,000 workers. “When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.” Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said. “Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.” Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved. But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State has also sued Amazon for this. Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws. Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond. PACE DRIVES INJURIES The worker justice group Warehouse Life has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group. Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible—or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this injury epidemic .” In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination. California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state fined Amazon $6 million for violating it. Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal. Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal. IS THERE A POLICY? Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from 40 states responded, and 81 described loss of a pregnancy. (To talk to Warehouse Life, schedule a call here .) Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mt. Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon Board of Directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record. Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said. When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is “Delay. Deny. Discipline.” MARCH ON H.R. The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the 5,000-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April. The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant. The union sent several workers to accompany her to H.R., saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections (see box at upper right) . The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.” “It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.” Pregnancy Rights It has been illegal to discriminate against pregnant workers since 1978, when feminist agitation won the Pregnancy Discrimination Act (under Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act), which says employers can’t discriminate based on pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. Before that, many employers had a policy of terminating workers when they got pregnant, and pregnant women often weren’t eligible for unemployment insurance. In 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act strengthened pregnancy rights. Now employers are required to make reasonable accommodations. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has found that reasonable accommodations which don’t require a doctor’s note include: a seat; additional breaks to eat, drink, or use the bathroom; adjusted uniforms and safety equipment; and changes to your job duties or your schedule to make it possible for you to keep working safely while you’re pregnant or recovering from a birth. Additional accommodations that might require a doctor’s note include limits on weight you have to lift, bending, and ladder use. “But you still have the right to get those accommodations quickly and have them implemented effectively,” said Katherine Greenberg, attorney with A Better Balance . “It is illegal for employers like Amazon to force workers to take a leave of absence if there’s an on-the-job accommodation that would keep them safe and allow them to keep working and earning an income,” said Greenberg. Also, employers can’t punish workers for asking for or needing accommodations. “If you need to pump milk for your baby, you have the right to take a lactation break without being punished for too much time off task,” said Greenberg. “Or if you experience a miscarriage and you need to miss work to recover, you have the right to take that time without being deducted UPT or assigned points for your absence.” Your state or city may have additional protections; check here . Have a question or concern about your pregnancy at Amazon? Schedule a call with Warehouse Life here .

articles.author: Laura O’Connor
articles.content: “This is a concerted effort to keep abortion out of the headlines and out of voters' calculus," said Vasquez-Giroux. “The plan is not to be better on abortion; it’s just to put it off until [these candidates] retain power.” Read more via Scalawag : Was Abortion the Swing Issue for Southern Voters? .
